standfirst: A nurse moves to the psychiatric ward and the show hands each hour to a different patient, with animation standing in for what illness feels like from the inside. It looks like comfort viewing and it is not. These six sit in the same key: institutional kindness, honestly costed.

picks.why: Medicine as a workplace rather than a crisis. Same pleasure in competent colleagues covering for each other, same episodic structure where a patient arrives and something small is repaired. Difference: it is genuinely comforting, and nobody on staff falls apart the way this show insists they do.

Junior staff being ground down and looking after each other anyway. The exhaustion is the subject in both, and both are exact about the hierarchy that produces it. Difference: obstetrics and comedy, so the tone stays light even when the hours are terrible.

Mental illness given a full production instead of a subplot. Both refuse to treat a diagnosis as a personality and both put a carer at the centre. Difference: it is a romance with fairytale styling, so the emotional register is much larger.

Small mercies performed as a job. Same structure of one story per episode, each about a person the system processed and nobody sat with. Difference: the dead are the clients, and the central relationship is a guardianship rather than a ward.

Burnout treated as an injury, not a weakness. Same patience with somebody who cannot go back to work yet and the same refusal to schedule a recovery. Difference: no medical setting, and the engine is two sisters swapping lives.

Care work as the whole plot. A hospice team, a damaged young man, and the slow discovery that being useful is a treatment. Difference: it is about dying rather than living with illness, and the pace is slower still.

against.title: It's Okay, That's Love
against.why: The obvious mental-health pairing from a decade earlier. Its clinical framing has aged badly and its romance drives everything, where this show keeps the ward at the centre.

against.title: Extraordinary Attorney Woo
against.why: Recommended because both are gentle and both concern neurology and stigma. That one is a legal procedural about competence being recognised; this one is about staff and patients getting through a shift.

against.title: Doctor Slump
against.why: Named as the other recent burnout drama. It plays depression as a romcom obstacle to be cleared by episode twelve, which is precisely the move this show declines to make.
